citation.title: The role of non-nation-state actors and side events in the international climate negotiations
citation.venue_or_publisher: Climate Policy 12(1), 23-37 (Taylor & Francis); published online 28 Jul 2011

question: Why non-nation-state actors (NNSAs) attend UN climate conferences (COPs), and to what extent official Side Events provide information relevant to the formal negotiations.
data: Survey of a sample of 117 official Side Events (56 of 200 at COP 13 Bali 2007, 61 of 181 at COP 14 Poznan 2008); 10 interviews with NNSA representatives; one interview with a UNFCCC Secretariat member; informal discussions; participant observation; eight written commentaries by researchers. Attendance figures (Figures 1-2) are from the UNFCCC Secretariat. COP 15 (2009) was not surveyed because of access restrictions.
method: Quantitative survey of Side Events (whether they referred to the formal negotiations, main topics, attendance) complemented by qualitative interviews, participant observation and commentaries. It does not count or classify business or fossil-fuel representatives in country delegations.

definitions.term: constituencies (observer groupings, including Business and Industry NGOs)
definitions.definition: Loose groups of like-minded observer organizations; the Business and Industry Non-Governmental Organizations constituency is one of the groupings, formed in 1992.
definitions.quote: Constituencies are loose groups of like-minded organizations, somewhat similar in nature to the negotiating coalitions that have been formed by countries.

proxies.indicator: Membership of the Business and Industry Non-Governmental Organizations constituency
proxies.quote: They currently include the Business and Industry Non-Governmental Organizations and the Environmental Non-Governmental Organizations, both formed in 1992

proxies.concept: business presence at the COP through other routes
proxies.indicator: Business attendees obtain passes through trade associations (stated by the authors, not measured)
proxies.quote: But business attendees can easily secure passes through other routes, typically trade associations.

findings.claim: Many national delegations admit NGO, municipal or business representatives into their delegations, which adds to the total attendance. No share or count of business members is given.
findings.quote: many national delegations also admit non-governmental organization (NGO), municipal or business representatives into their delegations, raising the total number even further.

findings.claim: Observers outnumbered national delegates at most COPs up to 2009.
findings.quote: observers have outnumbered delegates at the majority of COP meetings

findings.claim: At COP 15 (2009) the registered media, NGO and intergovernmental observer delegates numbered 16,700 against 10,600 country delegates.
Before 2010 observer organizations could nominate any number of representatives; from 2010 they were given a quota.
findings.quote: Before 2010, each registered observer organization was able to nominate any number of representatives to attend

findings.claim: Under UN rules businesses cannot register directly as observers, and the authors report that business attendees come through other routes such as trade associations.
findings.quote: businesses are not directly able to obtain a pass to attend the COP according to UN rules

findings.claim: Business and other non-state actors put pressure on governments, but the authors judge their influence to happen largely before the COP.
findings.quote: NNSAs (NGOs and industry associations, but especially businesses and local governments) apply important pressure on governments

findings.claim: Business Day, a Parallel Event organized by the WBCSD, was for business-to-business discussion; the Director said business lacked a voice at the COP.
findings.quote: we don’t have a good voice at the COP and wanted to organize a speciﬁc day

findings.claim: Just under 60% of Side Events at COP 13 and 75% at COP 14 made frequent or direct reference to the negotiations.
findings.quote: just under 60% of Side Events at COP 13 and 75% at COP 14 made frequent or direct reference to the negotiation process

limitations.point: The paper is about observer organizations and Side Events at COP 13-15 (2007-2009). It does not measure business or fossil-fuel presence in Party delegations, and does not define or identify fossil-fuel linked actors; nothing on Q2 or on classification methods.
Authors caution about the survey data because attendance depended on non-content factors.
limitations.quote: There are several reasons to be cautious about the survey data.

limitations.point: The survey could not be continued at COP 15 because of access restrictions, so it covers COP 13 and COP 14 only.
limitations.quote: it was decided to limit the survey to COP 13 and COP 14

limitations.point: Interviews are exploratory (10 interviews); the interviewee view that business has no formal channel was corrected by the authors, who note regular meetings with constituencies.
limitations.quote: although exploratory are nevertheless judged here to be worthwhile reporting due to the limited empirical research in this ﬁeld to date

limitations.point: The extracted file has an empty authors field and title 'untitled'; authors and title come from page 1-2 text. Figures 1-6 are images, so their values are not in the text; only figures given in prose are used. Peer review status is not stated in the text. No instructions addressed to a reader or an AI were found.
